'''Mary Jane West-Eberhard''' (born 1941<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wellenreuther |first1=Maren |author-link=Maren Wellenreuther |last2=Otto |first2=Sarah |year=2016 |title=Women in evolution–highlighting the changing face of evolutionary biology |journal=Evolutionary Applications |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=3–16 |doi=10.1111/eva.12343 |doi-access=free |pmc=4780375 |pmid=27087836 |bibcode=2016EvApp...9....3W |quote=For my generation–growing up in the 1950s (I was born in 1941)}}</ref>) is an American [[theoretical biology|theoretical biologist]] noted for arguing that [[phenotypic plasticity|phenotypic]] and developmental plasticity played a key role in shaping animal [[evolution]] and [[speciation]]. She is also an [[entomologist]] notable for her work on the behavior and evolution of [[wasp|social wasp]]s.

She is a member both of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 2005 she was elected to be a foreign member of the Italian [[Accademia dei Lincei]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://news.bio-medicine.org/biology-news-3/West-Eberhard-elected-to-the-Italian-Accademia-Nazionale-dei-Lincei-10581-1/ |title=West-Eberhard elected to the Italian Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei |access-date=2009-06-12 |archive-date=2011-07-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725080204/http://news.bio-medicine.org/biology-news-3/West-Eberhard-elected-to-the-Italian-Accademia-Nazionale-dei-Lincei-10581-1/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> She has been a past president (1991) of the [[Society for the Study of Evolution]].<ref name="humanrights">[http://www7.nationalacademies.org/HUMANRIGHTS/CHR_Vice_Chair_West-Eberhard.html   Mary Jane West-Eberhard, CHR Vice Chair] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090330063848/http://www7.nationalacademies.org/humanrights/CHR_Vice_Chair_West-Eberhard.html |date=2009-03-30 }}</ref> She won the 2003 R.R. Hawkins Award for the Outstanding Professional, Reference or Scholarly Work<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060505221429/http://www.pspcentral.org/awards/archive/winners_2003.doc R.R. Hawkins Award for the Outstanding Professional, Reference or Scholarly Work Press release]}}.</ref> for her book ''Developmental Plasticity and Evolution'' (618 pages).<ref name="WEbook03">West-Eberhard M-J. (2003). Developmental plasticity and evolution. Oxford University Press, New York. {{ISBN|978-0-19-512235-0}}</ref> In the same year she was the recipient of the [[Sewall Wright Award]].<ref name="Zuk">{{Citation |title=2003 Sewall Wright Award: Mary Jane West-Eberhard | author=Marlene Zuk | journal=American Naturalist | year=2004 | volume=163 | issue=1 | pages=i–ii | doi=10.1086/381946 | s2cid=82908880 }}</ref>  She has been selected as one of the 21 "Leaders in Animal Behavior".<ref>Drickamer L. Dewsbury S. (Dec 2009) Leaders in Animal Behaviour: The Second Generation. Cambridge University Press. [http://cambridge.org/us/catalogue/catalogue.asp?isbn=9780521741293]</ref>

She is engaged in long-term research projects at the [[Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute]] at the Escuela de Biologia, [[Universidad de Costa Rica]].

==Early life and education==
West-Eberhard's mother was a primary school teacher, and her father, a small-town businessman, and as parents they encouraged her curiosity. She went to school in Plymouth Community Schools, Plymouth, Michigan. She recalls of her high school that the best scientific training "was an English course on critical reading and writing, taught by the school librarian. Biology class was just a workbook, an enormous disappointment for me."<ref name="West-Eberhard MJ. 2009">{{cite journal | pmid = 19196328 | doi=10.1111/j.1525-142X.2008.00297.x | volume=11 | title=BIO | year=2009 | journal=Evol. Dev. | pages=8–10  | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ| issue=1 | s2cid=221678771 }} {{verify source |date=September 2019 |reason=This ref was deleted Special:Diff/864986225 by a bug in VisualEditor and later restored by a bot from the original cite located at Special:Permalink/846940030 cite #8 - verify the cite is accurate and delete this template. [[User:GreenC bot/Job 18]]}}</ref>

She did all her degrees at the [[University of Michigan]]. She did her bachelor's degree from University of Michigan in zoology in 1963. She earned her master's degree from the same place in zoology in 1964, and then her PhD (zoology) in 1967. There she was taught by [[Richard D. Alexander]] and had part-time employment in its [[Museums at the University of Michigan|Museum of Zoology]]. She records that "I also learned the excitement of being a sleuth in the university libraries where even an undergraduate could explore an idea beyond textbooks and could feel like a pioneer". She also corresponded with [[E. O. Wilson|Edward Wilson]] on trophic eggs in insects, and spent summers at [[Woods Hole]] and [[Cali]] in [[Colombia]].<ref name="West-Eberhard MJ. 2009"/>

She did postdoctoral work (1967–1969) at [[Harvard University]] with [[Howard Ensign Evans|Howard Evans]]. There she met her husband. She then spent the next ten years (1969–1979) as an associate in biology at the [[University of Valle]]. In 1973 she began an association with the [[Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute]] in [[Costa Rica]] which became a full-time employment in 1986.

==Social insects==
West-Eberhard has studied many species of social wasps such as ''[[Polistes fuscatus]]'', ''[[Polistes canadensis]]'', and ''[[Polistes erythrocephalus]].''<ref name = nelson>{{cite web |url=http://www.ots.ac.cr/rbt/attachments/volumes/vol18-1/07-Nelson-Polistes.pdf|title=Nesting habits and nest symbionts of Polistes erythrocephalus Latreille (Hymenoptera V'espidae) in Costa Rica|access-date=2014-10-14 |work=Biology |publisher=bio-nica.info }}</ref> Through her studies she has investigated why wasps evolved from being casteless and nestsharing casteless to becoming highly specialized [[eusocial]] species using comparative studies of tropical wasps ([[Hymenoptera]]). She has argued that origins of nonreproductive females in social wasps involves [[Mutualism (biology)|mutualism]] rather than only [[kin selection]] or parental manipulation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ | year = 1978 | title   =Temporary queens in metapolybia wasps: nonreproductive helpers without altruism?| journal = Science | volume = 200 | issue = 4340| pages = 441–443 | pmid = 17757302 | doi = 10.1126/science.200.4340.441 | bibcode = 1978Sci...200..441W | s2cid = 44353493 }}</ref>

Her work upon social insects has played an  important role in the development of her ideas upon [[phenotypic plasticity]].<ref>West-Eberhard MJ. (1975). [http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_1975_QRB_STRI.pdf The evolution of social behavior by kin selection]{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. Quart. Rev. Biol. 50(1):1-33.</ref><ref>West-Eberhard MJ. (1987). [http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_1987_F_Strategy_STRI.pdf Flexible strategy and social evolution]{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}., pp. 35-51 In Animal societies: Theories and facts, Y. Ito, J. L. Brown, and J. Kikkawa, eds., Japan Scientific Societies Press, Ltd., Tokyo. {{ISBN|978-4-7622-0514-9}}</ref> As she notes "From there I got interested in alternative phenotypes—alternative pathways and decision points during development, and their significance for evolution, especially for higher levels of organization, for speciation, and for macroevolutionary change without speciation."<ref name="West-Eberhard09Bio">{{cite journal | pmid = 19196328 | doi=10.1111/j.1525-142X.2008.00297.x | volume=11 | title=BIO | year=2009 | journal=Evol. Dev. | pages=8–10 | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ| issue=1 | s2cid=221678771 }}</ref>

==Phenotypic plasticity==
West-Eberhard has written from the mid-1980s upon  the role of "alternative phenotypes," such as [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphism]]s, [[polyphenism]]s, and context sensitive phenotype [[Biological life cycle|life history]] and  [[physiological]] traits.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ | year = 1986 | title = Alternative adaptations, speciation, and phylogeny | url = http://www.pubmedcentral.nih.gov/picrender.fcgi?artid=323081&blobtype=pdf | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 83 | issue = 5| pages = 1388–1392 | pmid = 16578790 | pmc = 323081 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.83.5.1388 | doi-access = free }}{{dead link|date=July 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ | year = 1989 | title = Phenotypic plasticity and the origins of diversity | url = http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_1989_Phenotypic_STRI.pdf | journal = Annu. Rev. Ecol. Syst. | volume = 20 | issue = 1 | pages = 249–278 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.es.20.110189.001341 | bibcode = 1989AnRES..20..249W }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url = http://www.pubmedcentral.nih.gov/picrender.fcgi?artid=33870&blobtype=pdf | pmid = 9671691 | volume=95 | title=Evolution in the light of developmental and cell biology, and vice versa | pmc=33870 | date=July 1998 | journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. | pages=8417–9  | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ | issue = 15 | doi=10.1073/pnas.95.15.8417| bibcode = 1998PNAS...95.8417W | doi-access = free }}{{dead link|date=July 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> This resulted in her 2003  book ''Developmental Plasticity and Evolution''.<ref name="WEbook03"/>

She argues that such alternative phenotypes are important since they can lead to novel traits, and then to [[genetic divergence]] and so speciation. Through alternative phenotypes environmental induction can take the lead in genetic evolution. Her book ''Developmental Plasticity and Evolution'' developed in detail how such environmental plasticity plays a key role in understanding the genetic theory of evolution. Her argument is full of examples from butterflies to elephants.

==Sexual and social selection==
West-Eberhard was among the first scientists<ref name="Zuk"/>  to reexamine [[Charles Darwin]]'s ideas in ''[[The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex]]'' about [[sexual selection]] and identify the key importance he gave to the "social competition for mates" as a factor in evolution<ref>West-Eberhard MJ. (1979). [http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_1979_SexualSel_Social.pdf Sexual selection, social competition, and evolution]{{Dead link|date=December 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. Proc. Amer. Phil. Soc. 51(4):222-234.</ref>    and [[speciation]].<ref>West-Eberhard MJ. (1983). [http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_1983_QRB_STRI.pdf Sexual selection, social competition, and speciation]{{Dead link|date=December 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. Quart. Rev. Biol. 58(2):155-183.</ref> She has noted how sexual selection can trap animals into sexual dimorphisms, to maintain separate sexes in [[sexual reproduction]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = West-Eberhard | first1 = MJ | year = 2005 | title = The maintenance of sex as a developmental trap due to sexual selection | url = http://stri.si.edu/publications/PDFs/West_Eberhard_2005_QRB_STRI.pdf | journal = Quarterly Review of Biology | volume = 80 | issue = 1 | pages = 47–53 | doi = 10.1086/431024 | pmid = 15884735 | s2cid = 7121799 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Other work==
As a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]], West-Eberhard has served for three terms on its Committee on Human Rights.<ref name="humanrights"/><ref>National Academy of Sciences Committee on Human Rights and Institute of Medicine Committee on Health and Human Rights. (1992). [http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=2038  Scientists and Human Rights in Guatemala: Report of a Delegation]. National Academy Press Washington, D.C. National Academy Press Washington, D.C.</ref> She has also been noted as "active in promoting the careers of young scientists, particularly those doing work in Latin America".<ref name="Zuk"/>

Since 2013, West-Eberhard has been listed on the advisory council of the [[National Center for Science Education]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |title=Advisory Council |website=ncse.com |publisher=[[National Center for Science Education]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130810112828/https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |archive-date=2013-08-10 |access-date=2018-10-30|date=2008-07-15 }}</ref>
